doc.title: Loren Schoenberg interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019

chapter: Benny Goodman and the big band
title: Goodman calls: cataloguing his library for the New York Public Library
summary: Goodman calls in his fourth year of college to document his library for the New York Public Library; Schoenberg leaves school.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: And understanding who Nick Payton is. You know what I mean. Or who Wynton Marsalis is. Or whom you are or I am or any of these people are. When you start to put it in that context. So that happened in those years. And then in the meantime I had mentioned Russ Connor before and BG on the Record and the Benny Goodman biodiscography. So I had been very much pursuing that stuff too, collecting records, and I was doing radio shows in college and all this kind of stuff, like a lot of us did. And because I knew Hank Jones as an idol and as somebody who my parents loved and who would get me into gigs to see, I was actually around backstage at some Benny Goodman concerts with Urbie Green and Benny and Bucky Pizzarelli and Hank and all those people, just as a kid, just sitting there just quiet — I don’t know how quiet I was, but just sitting there kind of looking and never in a million years thinking that I could play with them but that I was just lucky to be there. And so there was a little more of a connection around the Benny Goodman circle of things. Scott Hamilton had come to New York at that time and was just unbelievable. I mean that’s another fascinating thing what Scott did and his band of musicians. And then, in my fourth year of college, I got a call from Benny Goodman and I mean I felt like saying, I mean, “This is Benny Goodman” and I was going to say I’m Artie Shaw and hang up the phone. And it turns out that he was donating his music library to the New York Public Library. And he had contacted Russ Connor, the guy who wrote the book about him, and he said Russ, I need someone to write the accompanying I think they call it a provenance or something, the accompanying monograph or little book about these arrangements. In other words when were they written and what key were they in and were they recorded. And Russ, who worked at the Federal Reserve Bank in Philadelphia, he didn’t have time. He said well there’s this crazy © Fillius Jazz Archive -19-

kid in New York you know, who you know is always collecting your records. Maybe he might know. And he’s a musician. So I left school. I don’t have a bachelor’s degree. I’m one of the rare people who wound up teaching in the master’s — I taught in the graduate school of the school I never graduated from, which I guess you can’t do anymore, right?
